Title: The Sun Never Set (Part 2 of 10): Sugar, Slavery and Company Men, 1660–1756

Summary: Between the Restoration of Charles II and the eve of the Seven Years' War, England and then Great Britain built an Atlantic economy on sugar and enslaved African labour, created the state of Great Britain, and watched the Mughal Empire fragment. This post lines up the slave trade, the Jacobite risings, Maroon wars and the East India Company's early stumbles against the wider world of 1660 to 1756.

---

## The big picture

In 1660 England had scattered colonies and trading posts. By 1756 Great Britain (created in 1707) had the largest navy in the world, thirteen mainland American colonies, rich sugar islands in the Caribbean, and was the leading carrier of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic. In India the East India Company was still a trader, not a ruler, but the collapse of central Mughal authority after 1707 was opening a door.

Three engines drove this period:

- **Sugar and slavery.** Caribbean sugar was the most valuable colonial product, and it ran on enslaved labour.
- **The fiscal-military state.** After 1688 Britain created the Bank of England (1694) and a national debt, which let it borrow and fight wars on a scale its rivals struggled to match.
- **Rivalry with France.** From 1689 to 1815 Britain and France fought seven major wars. Historians call it the "Second Hundred Years' War".

## Main timeline (1660–1713)

| Year | What happened | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1660 | Company of Royal Adventurers into Africa chartered, led by the King's brother James | The Crown itself invests in the slave trade |
| 1661 | Bombay and Tangier come to England as the dowry of Catherine of Braganza | Bombay is handed to the EIC in 1668; Tangier is abandoned in 1684 |
| 1664 | New Amsterdam taken from the Dutch and renamed New York | Links New England to the Chesapeake colonies |
| 1665–1667 | Second Anglo-Dutch War (and the Great Plague, 1665; Great Fire of London, 1666) | The Dutch raid the Medway in 1667, a humiliation, but England keeps New York |
| 1670 | Hudson's Bay Company chartered | Claims a huge share of today's Canada for the fur trade |
| 1672 | Royal African Company (RAC) founded | Between 1672 and 1731 it shipped more enslaved Africans to the Americas than any other single institution in the trade |
| 1675–1676 | King Philip's War (Metacom's War) in New England | Proportionally one of the deadliest wars in American history |
| 1676 | Bacon's Rebellion in Virginia | Colonists rebel against the governor; planters shift further from indentured servants to enslaved Africans |
| 1686–1690 | "Child's War": the EIC goes to war with the Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb | The Company **loses** and has to beg for pardon. A reminder of who held power in India |
| 1688 | Glorious Revolution; William III and Mary II replace James II | Parliament gains control of taxation and the army |
| 1690 | Calcutta founded by Job Charnock; Battle of the Boyne in Ireland | Calcutta becomes the Company's future capital; the Boyne secures Protestant rule in Ireland |
| 1695 onwards | Penal Laws in Ireland restrict Catholics' rights to land, office and education | Shapes Irish society for over a century |
| 1694 | Bank of England founded | Makes long wars affordable |
| 1698 | RAC monopoly ends; the slave trade is opened to all English merchants | The trade grows rapidly; Bristol and later Liverpool boom |
| 1698–1700 | Scotland's Darien scheme in Panama collapses | Scotland loses a large share of its liquid capital, one push toward union |
| 1707 | Acts of Union: England and Scotland become Great Britain | Scots are soon over-represented in the empire's army, trade and administration |
| 1701–1714 | War of the Spanish Succession | Britain fights France and Spain across Europe and the Americas |
| 1713 | Treaty of Utrecht | Britain gains Gibraltar, Minorca, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, Hudson Bay, St Kitts and the Asiento (the right to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish America) |

## Main timeline (1714–1756)

| Year | What happened | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1714 | George I of Hanover becomes king | Hanoverian dynasty begins |
| 1715 | First major Jacobite rising (the "Fifteen") | Supporters of the Stuart line fail in Scotland |
| 1717 | Mughal Emperor Farrukhsiyar grants the EIC duty-free trade in Bengal | A trade privilege the Company later abuses heavily |
| 1720 | South Sea Bubble bursts | The South Sea Company held the Asiento; its share price collapse ruins many investors |
| 1732 | Georgia chartered | The last of the thirteen mainland colonies |
| 1739 | Treaties between Britain and the Jamaican Maroons | Britain, unable to defeat them, recognises Maroon self-government in return for help catching runaways |
| 1739–1748 | War of Jenkins' Ear, merging into the War of the Austrian Succession | Fought from the Caribbean to India |
| 1745 | New England forces take the French fortress of Louisbourg | Handed back in 1748, to the colonists' anger |
| 1745–1746 | The "Forty-Five": Charles Edward Stuart's Jacobite rising; defeated at Culloden | Brutal repression of the Highlands; many Highlanders later join the British Army and settle the colonies |
| 1746 | French capture Madras | Returned in 1748 in exchange for Louisbourg |
| 1746–1754 | First and Second Carnatic Wars in south India | Britain and France fight through Indian proxy rulers; Robert Clive makes his name at Arcot (1751) |
| 1749 | Halifax founded in Nova Scotia | British military base facing French Louisbourg |
| 1754 | Fighting starts in the Ohio Valley, involving a young George Washington | The first shots of what becomes the Seven Years' War |
| 1755 | Expulsion of the Acadians from Nova Scotia begins; Braddock's army destroyed near Fort Duquesne | Over the following years roughly 10,000 Acadians are deported |

| Years | Event | Region |
|---|---|---|
| 1661–1722 | Kangxi Emperor; Qing China at its height | China |
| 1680 | Pueblo Revolt expels the Spanish from New Mexico for 12 years | North America |
| 1683 | Ottoman siege of Vienna fails; long Ottoman retreat in Europe begins | Central Europe |
| 1685 | Louis XIV revokes the Edict of Nantes; Huguenots flee, many to England and its colonies | France |
| 1687 | Newton's *Principia* published | Europe |
| 1689 | Treaty of Nerchinsk between Russia and Qing China | Eurasia |
| 1692 | Salem witch trials | Massachusetts |
| 1703 | Peter the Great founds St Petersburg | Russia |
| 1707 | Death of Aurangzeb; Mughal central authority begins to break up | India (same year as the Act of Union) |
| 1720s–1740s | Rise of the Maratha Confederacy across central India | India |
| 1739 | Nadir Shah of Persia sacks Delhi and carries off the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond | India (same year as the Maroon treaties and Stono) |
| 1740–1786 | Frederick the Great makes Prussia a major power | Europe |
| 1744 | Alliance of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab and Muhammad ibn Saud | Arabia (the origin of the Saudi state) |
| 1747 | Ahmad Shah Durrani founds the Afghan Durrani Empire | Afghanistan |
| 1752 | Britain switches to the Gregorian calendar; eleven days are skipped | Britain |
| 1755 | Lisbon earthquake | Portugal |

## Resistance: revolts against slavery and colonial rule

The Caribbean was the most violent part of the early empire, with frequent conspiracies and risings by enslaved people. This table lists the best documented.

| Years | Revolt | Where | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1675–1676 | King Philip's War (Metacom) | New England | Wampanoag and allies defeated; survivors sold into Caribbean slavery |
| 1675 and 1692 | Planned slave revolts uncovered | Barbados | Dozens executed |
| 1712 | New York slave revolt | New York | About two dozen executed |
| 1715–1717 | Yamasee War | South Carolina | Nearly destroyed the colony before the Yamasee were defeated |
| c.1728–1739 | First Maroon War | Jamaica | Maroons under Cudjoe and Nanny win treaties of autonomy |
| 1733–1734 | St John slave revolt (a Danish colony) | Virgin Islands | Shows revolts were Caribbean-wide, not only British |
| 1736 | Planned rising (Prince Klaas / Court) | Antigua | Uncovered; 88 executed, according to the commonly cited figure |
| 1739 | Stono Rebellion | South Carolina | Largest slave revolt in the mainland colonies before 1776; led to the Negro Act of 1740 |
| 1741 | New York conspiracy trials | New York | Over 30 executed on thin evidence |
| 1715, 1745 | Jacobite risings | Scotland and England | Defeated; Highland clan system dismantled after 1746 |

## Things that happened at the same time

- **1707.** Aurangzeb died and Great Britain was created in the same year. One great state began to fragment just as another was consolidating.
- **1739.** In the same year: Nadir Shah sacked Delhi, the Stono Rebellion broke out in South Carolina, Britain signed peace treaties with the Jamaican Maroons, and the War of Jenkins' Ear began. Each was a sign of a shifting balance of power.
- **1686–1690.** At the same time as the Glorious Revolution in London, the East India Company was losing a war against the Mughals. The idea that British power in India was always inevitable does not survive this period.
- **1745–1746.** While Bonnie Prince Charlie marched south toward Derby, the French were preparing to take Madras. The British state was fighting off a rebellion at home and a rival abroad at the same time.

## Sources and flags

- David Eltis and David Richardson, *Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade* (2010), and the Slave Voyages database: https://www.slavevoyages.org
- P. J. Marshall (ed.), *The Oxford History of the British Empire, Volume II: The Eighteenth Century* (1998).
- William Dalrymple, *The Anarchy* (2019), on the Child's War and Mughal decline.
- Richard Gott, *Britain's Empire: Resistance, Repression and Revolt* (2011), for many of the revolts listed.
- Linda Colley, *Britons: Forging the Nation 1707–1837* (1992), on the Union and national identity.
- **Flag:** Execution and death tolls for slave conspiracies (Antigua 1736, New York 1741) come from colonial trial records and are commonly cited but sometimes vary between sources. The Acadian deportation total is an approximation; estimates usually range from about 10,000 to 11,500 over 1755–1764.
